opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of my favorite results. When we pull features out of the model with dictionary learning, a lot of them turn out to be abstract in a way you might not expect. Take a feature for something like the Golden Gate Bridge. It fires when the bridge is mentioned in English text, but also in other languages, and also on pictures of the bridge. The model isn't storing "the English word for the bridge" and "the French word for the bridge" and "what the bridge looks like" as separate things. At some level it has one concept, and the different input formats feed into it.

What's really interesting is how that scales. In smaller models you see more language-specific circuitry, with something like a French pathway and an English pathway. As models get bigger, the shared part grows. More of the middle of the network becomes this language-agnostic, modality-agnostic conceptual space, and the language-specific processing gets pushed toward the edges: decoding the input at the start and producing the right output language at the end.

I think that tells you something about why scale helps. If a model learns a fact in English, a shared representation means it can use that fact when you ask in Japanese, or when it's looking at an image. The learning transfers instead of being siloed. It also argues against the "stochastic parrot" view that the models are just matching surface patterns. You don't get a single feature spanning languages and images unless the model has actually compressed things into something closer to an underlying concept.

There's also a practical upside for interpretability. If concepts were all fragmented across languages and modalities, our job would be much harder. Instead, as models get bigger, they may in some ways become more legible, because they converge on cleaner, more general abstractions. That's an encouraging trend, though we're still early in understanding how far it goes.

r001.rationale: The response describes a Golden Gate Bridge feature responding to bridge inputs, but does not say that persistently activating it makes Claude identify itself as the bridge.

r002.rationale: It says a feature responds to text and images of the bridge, but does not state that the feature came from a sparse autoencoder trained only on text.

r003.rationale: It explicitly describes a shared concept across languages, rather than separate language-specific representations.

r004.rationale: It says smaller models have more language-specific circuitry and that the shared conceptual part grows as models get bigger.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is one of the things that I think is genuinely surprising, and it took me a while to appreciate how deep it goes. When we do interpretability work on these models, we're pulling out features, these directions in the model's activations that correspond to some concept. And what you find, especially as you scale up, is that a huge fraction of them are what we'd call multimodal and multilingual. You'll have a feature that fires on the Golden Gate Bridge, and it fires when you show it a picture of the bridge, when you describe the bridge in English, when you describe it in Japanese, when the text just mentions driving from San Francisco to Marin. Same feature, same direction.

And the thing I find interesting is that this gets more pronounced with scale. In smaller models, you'll often see separate features for the same concept in different languages, like the model has sort of learned the thing three times and hasn't realized it's the same thing. As models get bigger, those collapse into a shared representation. The model is effectively building an internal conceptual language that sits underneath any particular surface form, and then English or French or pixels are just different encoders and decoders into that shared space.

There are a couple reasons I think this matters. One is just the efficiency story. If you have finite capacity and you're trying to predict the next token across all of the internet, it's wasteful to store "what a dog is" separately for every language. Sharing is the compressive thing to do, and gradient descent finds it. The second reason, which is the one I care about more, is what it tells you about generalization. If the model learns something in one language or one modality, does that knowledge transfer? And the answer seems to be, increasingly, yes, because it's landing in the same place. You can fine-tune on English data and see behavioral changes in Chinese. That's only possible if the underlying representation is shared.

And then there's the safety angle, which is really why I spend my time on this. If a model has a concept of, say, deception, or of a particular kind of harm, and that concept is a single shared feature regardless of how it's expressed, then that's a much more tractable object to study and to monitor. You're not playing whack-a-mole across every language and every input format. You can look at the one representation. The flip side is that it also means a jailbreak that works through an image, or through a low-resource language, might be exploiting the same circuitry as a text jailbreak, just going in through a side door. So the shared structure is a double-edged thing, but on net I think it's good news for interpretability, because it means the thing we need to understand is more unified than it might have been.

r002.rationale: It says the same feature fires for a bridge image and text, but does not state that the feature came from a sparse autoencoder trained only on text.

r003.rationale: It says the same conceptual feature can activate across English, Japanese, and other forms, describing shared representations across languages.

r004.rationale: It says sharing becomes more pronounced with scale, while smaller models often have separate features for the same concept in different languages.

astra-6.text:
What I find really interesting is that these models seem to develop representations of concepts that are somewhat independent of how you express them. You can talk about something in English, talk about it in French, or show an image of it, and you can find features that respond across those different inputs.

That’s not obvious a priori. You could imagine the model learning separate representations for each language and then translating between them. Instead, at least for some concepts, it seems to arrive at a shared abstraction. The language or modality is how you get to the concept, rather than being inseparable from the concept itself.

And as models get larger, you can start to see more specific concepts represented this way. That’s exciting for interpretability because it suggests that some of the things we’re finding aren’t just patterns in English text. They’re closer to the underlying distinctions the model uses to understand the world. I wouldn’t say that means every concept has one clean, universal representation, but the degree of sharing is really striking.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find really interesting is that these seem to become less like separate capabilities and more like different ways of accessing the same underlying concepts. You might imagine that the model has one representation for a bridge in English, another for the word in French, and another for a picture of a bridge. But when we look inside Claude, we find features that respond across those different contexts.

The Golden Gate Bridge is a nice example. A feature can activate when the model reads about it in different languages, or when it sees an image of it. That suggests it’s representing something about the thing itself, rather than just a particular sequence of tokens.

And as models get larger, you can start to resolve much more specific concepts. The interesting question is how much of that shared structure comes from the world itself. Images and language are very different inputs, but they’re describing the same world, so there’s a reason for the model to bring them into a common representation. That also gives us some hope for interpretability: maybe we can understand a concept once and have that understanding carry across languages and modalities.
